It then gives two concrete ways to save lead time (group sessions and a short scorecard) and a fallback if the lead can't give even 5 hours. B has useful extras, such as a follow-up session, a worked example, tying results to a metric the VP already tracks and checking for non-training causes. But it only mentions the 15-hour figure in passing, and it adds more scope than the request needed. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend B and reduce the lead's load to about 5 hours with peer role-plays and a short scorecard. A adds useful extras, such as a follow-up session and checking for causes outside training, but it only implies the 15-hour figure, its offer to the VP is vaguer and uses placeholder metrics, and its claim that a same-day score can't show the skill will last is a weaker argument.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both recommend B, explain that a multiple-choice test checks recognition rather than live production, and calculate the 15 hours correctly. It also adds a scenario quiz and a plan to measure results against a baseline the team already tracks. A's ideas (triads, recordings, a facts check and a fallback) are solid, but its 60–70% reduction is a loose estimate rather than a worked-out schedule. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend B and make the same core point: a multiple-choice test shows whether a rep can recognize a good answer, not whether they can give one out loud. Answer B offers more concrete ways to keep scale (peer triads, recorded sessions reviewed later, a facts-only auto-scored check) plus a fallback if the lead has no time; its facts-only quiz also fits its own argument better than A's 'what do you say next' scenario quiz.
